newsitem.title: USA: USDA lifts Karnal bunt restrictions in Southeast.
newsitem.headline: USDA lifts Karnal bunt restrictions in Southeast.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department said Monday it was lifting all restrictions for the wheat fungus Karnal bunt in the U.S. Southeast.
"We've extensively studied the situation in the Southeast and have concluded Karnal bunt is not present there," said Terry Medley, administrator of USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

USDA had set quarantines in about two dozen premises, such as farms and grain elevators, in the Southeast after Karnal bunt-like spores were detected. The department said the quarantines would be lifted immediately.

"We've determined that there is no Karnal bunt associated with any of the positive spore detections we've discovered in the Southeast... it's all rye grass smut and rye grass is of no concern to us," said APHIS official Charles Schwalbe.
The department said last week its Karnal bunt testing in the Southeast portion of the nation had been called into question by the discovery a ryegrass smut with spores similiar to the Karnal bunt.
The grain industry welcomed Monday's news. An industry official said the Karnal bunt scare in the Southeast had disrupted markets and had been a "horrible money loser."
But the official also noted that the wheat fungus is a big export issue, and did not criticize the department for its initial actions in Southeast, saying, "the government has to be careful."
USDA said it based its decision on the fact that bunted wheat kernels were not found in any samples in the Southeast, whereas contamination with bunted ryegrass kernels was common.
Researchers have shown that spores from ryegrass do not infect wheat.

A national survey had detected karnal-bunt like teliospores, the causal agent for the fungus, in grain samples from several counties in Alabama, Florida, Georgia and Tennessee. Wheat seed contaminated with these spores was also planted in South Carolina.
The department began the nationwide survey for Karnal bunt last summer after parts of California, Arizona, Texas and New Mexico were quarantined because of the fungus.

Karnal bunt, also called Stinking Smut, makes wheat smell bad and reduces yields and quality. Many nations refuse to accept wheat that contains the fungus. The U.S. persuaded customers to continue to buy U.S. grain by issuing documents to prove the wheat did not come from an infected area.
USDA said in the near future it would publish a standard for determining the presence of Karnal bunt that would apply to all parts of the country.

"Establishing this standard will ensure that all U.S. wheat producers and handlers are treated equitably with regard to Karnal bunt and that U.S. wheat has necessary certification to remain competitive in global markets," assistant secretary for marketing and regulatory programs Michael Dunn said in a statement.
